before.exam_tip_html: In Section B, you are not being asked to tell the story. The examiner wants you to analyse and evaluate specific performance and design choices. Always use the SEAS paragraph structure: State what you saw, Explain why it was effective using drama terminology, describe the Audience impact, and Suggest a development. Remember — 10 of the 30 marks are specifically for using drama terminology, so make every sentence count.

When analysing the Diane Nash and CJ Reminder scenes, always identify the contrast between characters. Examiners reward answers that compare two performers’ techniques side by side. For example: “Diane Nash remained stoic with strong posture, whereas the US representative used quick, exaggerated movements. This contrast highlighted Nash’s unshakeable conviction versus the representative’s growing desperation.” Showing you can identify contrasts demonstrates sophisticated understanding of performance skills.

When answering a directing question, structure your response around three areas: performance (how would the actors use voice and physicality?), design (what lighting, sound, set, and costume choices would support the scene?), and conventions (which dramatic conventions are at work and what is their effect on the audience?). Always explain the impact on the audience — why does each choice matter? The examiner wants to see that you understand not just what would happen on stage, but why it would be effective.
